item.title: Image of the week: El Nino as seen from Sentinel-3

item.page_text:
The image shows how nighttime sea surface temperatures from 26 October to 1 November 2026 differed from the 1991–2020 average for the same week. Red areas were warmer than normal, and blue areas were cooler.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which the tropical Pacific Ocean becomes unusually warm every few years. Weakening trade winds let warm water spread east, changing weather patterns around the world. A very strong El Niño can shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather.
In the image, a band of red can be seen stretching along the equator from the central Pacific to South America, where the sea is up to 4°C warmer than normal. The warmth is strongest off Ecuador and Peru, replacing the cold water that usually rises to the surface there.
This anomaly image was produced using data from the Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer (SLSTR) on the Sentinel-3A- and B satellites.
The Sentinel-3 satellites observe the Earth’s oceans, as well as land, ice and atmosphere. The series began in 2016 and its data cover the entire planet and can reach users within three hours of collection.
The third satellite in the Sentinel-3 constellation - Sentinel-3C - was launched two months ago on 15 September and is already delivering images from its SLSTR instrument.
Sentinel-3C will ensure these vital data streams continue well into the 2030s. Once commissioning is complete, Sentinel-3C will take over from Sentinel-3A, while some Sentinel-3A observation capabilities will remain in operations.
Weekly nighttime sea surface temperature anomaly for 26 October to 1 November 2026, relative to the 1991–2020 climate normal.
The image was produced with data from the SLSTR instruments onboard the Copernicus Sentinel-3A and -B satellites.
EUMETSAT operates the Sentinel-3 satellites, in cooperation with ESA, and delivers the marine and atmospheric data on behalf of the European Union.

item.title: Madrid's Architectural Time Machine
item.summary: This year building-age maps have really come to life, with a new generation of 3D animated maps showing cities growing decade by decade. Block and Paper have been leading the way, creating animated building-age maps of cities around the world. Their approach has since inspired others, including Every Building in Los Angeles County and Paris, Building by Building . Now Carreteras y hospitales has brought this new approach to the Spanish capital with a building-age map of Madrid. Press play and you can watch the city grow, as colour-coded buildings appear according to the year they were constructed. The animation allows you to trace Madrid's expansion from its historic centre through its 20th-century growth and more recent developments. It is important to remember, however, that these building-age maps only show the age of the surviving building stock. They don't reveal where older buildings have been demolished and replaced by newer constructions. As a result, they can never paint a complete picture of how a city has developed over time; they show only the history of the buildings that still exist today. Nevertheless, they are great tools for discovering the historic parts of cities

item.title: New tool for flood runoff prediction, driven by Sentinel-2 and tested in Ethiopia
item.summary: New tool for flood runoff prediction, driven by Sentinel-2 and tested in Ethiopia ... Sentinel-2 imagery, CHIRPS rainfall from satellites, and ...
item.page_text:
Funded by the ESA-Future Earth Joint Program, a team in Ethiopia are building a flood warning system for farmers
A team of researchers from Haramaya University in eastern Ethiopia are empowering small-holdings farmers, local planners, and decision makers, through new insights on flood event risks in the near future and upcoming decades. The first paper from the project supported by the ESA-Future Earth Joint Program presents a GIS toolbox for estimating flood runoff, with initial conditions for the model fed by opensource satellite data. This enables rapid flood predictions that can be updated with new satellite information, as well as modelling of possible climate-driven changes to flood runoff patterns in later decades.
The Awash and Wabi Shebelle river basins in Eastern Ethiopia experience frequent and sometimes highly damaging floods each year, but these events happen at varying timescales, locations and durations, making them hard to predict seasonally. On-the-ground information about these floods is hard to come by, with gauging stations few and far between. And a changing climate with worsening monsoons, and growing urban developments responding to an expanding population, are putting residents and farmland at an even greater risk of damage.
This situation has motivated the group from Haramaya University to develop a new set of tools for delivering flood warnings in a timely and accessible manner, using Earth Observation in place of traditional in situ discharge records.
The open-source tool is based on a widely used model, the Soil Conservation Service Curve Number (SCS-CN), originally developed by the US Department of Agriculture in the 1950s. The model calculates the proportion of storm rainfall that runs off the land and contributes to flooding, versus sinking into the ground. But existing applications of the SCS-CN face limitations, namely that they don't include existing soil moisture conditions, complete event catalogues, or sub-basin outputs in a single workflow, and flooding thresholds are not specific to a location's history. The tool developed by Kalid Hassen Yasin and Beyan Ahmed Yuya addresses these points across data-scarce Ethiopian floodplains, using publicly available Sentinel-2 imagery, CHIRPS rainfall from satellites, and land-based climate reanalyses from ECMWF's ERA5.
The satellite-driven approach was tested using 587 rainfall events recorded between 2010 and 2023 across eastern Ethiopia, alongside documented historical floods such as the April 2016 Jijiga event and 2023 East Africa rain season . Of these, the GIS tool (using locally calibrated runoff limits) successfully identified 13 out of 16 documented floods while producing approximately 62% fewer false alarms than the existing regional rainfall threshold, at the same detection rate. This suggests that locally tailored warning criteria could help disaster-risk managers issue more targeted alerts, and potentially reduce unnecessary warnings.
Almost all the recorded rainfall events occurred under dry initial conditions, reflecting the semi-arid environment of eastern Ethiopia. Under these conditions, the runoff-based approach performed similarly to using basin-averaged rainfall alone. So more sophisticated modelling did not necessarily provide better flood detection in every setting.
Nevertheless, the open-source toolbox offers additional benefits, including spatially distributed runoff estimates and a systematic approach to calibrating warning thresholds. The findings also highlight the importance of local calibration, as runoff estimates and alert thresholds are sensitive to modelling assumptions.
Combining ground observations with satellite data offers a promising way forward. Satellite rainfall observations could help extend geographical coverage beyond the existing network of ground-based rainfall gauges, and fill gaps in historical records. This is especially key for neighbouring regions in Africa, who suffer from similar rainfall events and limited monitoring networks. Satellite radar observations (SAR) could provide independent information on the extent of flooding, helping validate and improve the modelling approach.
The work by Haramaya University highlights an opportunity for combining satellite Earth observation, ground measurements, and relatively simple hydrological models, to strengthen local disaster-risk management across East Africa.
In October 2026, Kalid Hassen Yasin presented the paper at the 18th GeoMundus International Conference on Geospatial Intelligence for Disaster Resilience. Held this year at Universitat Jaume I in Castellón de la Plana, Spain, the conference is organised by students of the Erasmus Mundus Master in Geospatial Technologies, and unites researchers, practitioners, and students from across the globe.
For his talk "An integrated ArcGIS Python toolbox for SCS-CN event runoff estimation and flood screening in data-scarce Ethiopian basins", Kalid received the Best Oral Presentation award, which both affirms the impact and interest in the research, and helps put tools to support Africa's flood warnings on the map.
The next steps in the project will be to investigate past and future flood susceptibility in the region using machine learning techniques and CMIP climate projections, and to characterise extreme rainfall events in major Ethiopian cities to understand their impacts on infrastructure and planning. More results from the project will also be presented at the 4th International GORILLA Conference in Uganda in December 2026.

In particular, one of the areas of damage is located near the attachment point of the bridge’s last remaining arch.
As the publication notes, following strike on the night of November 19 , rail traffic across the bridge was once again suspended. This occurred after rail traffic had been briefly resumed following the second attack.

item.title: What can satellites see when they look at Europe's forests? - Phys.org
item.summary: ... sentinel-2 data" (European Journal of Remote Sensing), D'Amico reconstructed the pest's spread between 2017 and 2025 using years of Sentinel-2 ...
item.page_text:
edited by Sadie Harley , 																								reviewed by Andrew Zinin
This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted
														the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:
Four new studies show how Earth observation has become an everyday instrument for watching and protecting the continent's forests and green spaces, from a single city park to the whole of Europe.
Europe's forests and urban greenery are under mounting pressure. Warming, drought, invasive pests and increasingly frequent disturbances are reshaping them faster than ground surveys alone can follow. To protect these ecosystems, we first have to be able to see them at every scale, from a single stretch of coastal pine to the entire continent.
This is where Earth observation has quietly become indispensable. Four recent studies show just how much, and how differently, satellites can now work for forests and green spaces. Produced in part by the same connected community of European researchers, together they answer one simple question: what, exactly, can satellites do?
The first job is also the most easily misjudged: measuring the green around us. In "Integrating earth observation and graph theory to evaluate urban green spaces connectivity across European capitals" ( Landscape Ecology ), a team led by researchers from the University of Florence mapped vegetation across 28 European capitals at 10-meter (33-foot) resolution and analyzed it with graph theory, finding that how much green a city has is a misleading measure.
A capital can be rich in parks yet leave them as isolated fragments, while another weaves its green into a continuous, functioning network.
"Satellites let us view urban green spaces as a connected system rather than isolated parks or trees," says Giovanni D'Amico, a co-author of the study.
"From above, we can measure how green areas are distributed and connected across an entire city, helping planners identify gaps, barriers and strategic areas where interventions could strengthen ecological connectivity and make urban nature more resilient."
From taking stock of the green we have, satellites turn to tracking a specific threat.
Along the coast of Campania, the stone pines (Pinus pinea) that frame the Italian shoreline are being killed by Toumeyella parvicornis, an invasive scale insect first recorded in the region in 2014. In "Spatio-temporal assessment of Toumeyella parvicornis spread in mediterranean coastal pine forests through sentinel-2 data" ( European Journal of Remote Sensing ), D'Amico reconstructed the pest's spread between 2017 and 2025 using years of Sentinel-2 imagery and explainable artificial intelligence, building maps reliable enough to anticipate where it is likely to strike next.
"Field surveys are essential, but they cover limited areas and often detect damage only after it becomes visible on the ground," he explains.
"Satellite observations make it possible to monitor large areas repeatedly and consistently, highlighting changes in vegetation condition and the spatial progression of the infestation, and therefore helping identify where impacts are emerging and where field inspections and management actions should be prioritized."
The risk is largely driven by contagion: pines are most exposed where a stressed canopy sits close to existing outbreaks.
One pest on one coastline raises a continental question: which forests are disturbances actually hitting?

        innovations, and research that matter— daily or weekly .
To work at that scale, "Natural disturbances from bark beetle outbreaks and windthrow increasingly affect Europe's most mature and carbon-rich forests" ( Biogeosciences ), led by the GFZ Helmholtz Center in Potsdam, combined three decades of satellite-derived maps of disturbance, biomass and tree species with data on forest age. What it reveals is not simply that disturbances are increasing, but that they are increasingly selective.
"Disturbances are not only increasing; they are also increasingly affecting Europe's older, most carbon-rich forests," says Simon Besnard—a change "very hard to capture from ground measurements alone."
The disturbed area of forest over 60 years old has nearly tripled since 2010, and the damage is concentrating on the densest, most carbon-rich stands, enough that, if the trend holds, natural disturbances could expose carbon equivalent to around 20% of Europe's forest carbon sink by 2040.
"This matters because these forests hold a disproportionate share of the continent's carbon," he adds. "Losing them to climate-sensitive disturbances such as bark beetle outbreaks could substantially weaken the forest carbon sink that Europe relies on to meet its climate ambitions."
And once a forest is hit, what does the damage leave behind?
Finally, satellites can capture a consequence that is invisible on the ground. In "Disturbance characteristics and forest properties regulate surface warming and recovery across Europe" ( Nature Geoscience ), researchers combined Landsat measurements of summer land-surface temperature with a Europe-wide disturbance atlas, finding that disturbed forest patches stay, on average, 1.70 °C warmer than nearby intact forest: a local surface signal, not a rise in regional air temperature, but one that can last for years and shape how forests regrow.
The warming is strongest where canopy loss is most severe, and in plantations, which also recover more slowly than natural forests. The reassuring part: more than 82% of it fades within a decade.
"Forest management can influence the size and duration of this local heat footprint," says Saverio Francini. "Limiting unnecessarily large canopy openings and keeping forests structurally complex can help moderate

item.page_text:
Ukraine has partially destroyed a key bridge to Crimea, increasing pressure on Russia's supply lines in southern and eastern Ukraine.
Ukraine has partially destroyed a key bridge to Crimea, increasing pressure on Russia’s supply lines in southern and eastern Ukraine. Although the bridge attacks are not decisive, they disrupt Russia’s logistics, which could be hard to manage. This action underscores Ukraine’s ability to target Russian logistics while Moscow’s advances on the battlefield slow down.
President Putin claimed the bridge was only for civilian use and threatened retaliation. In response, Russia launched missile attacks that damaged bridges in Ukraine’s capital. This week’s destruction of the bridge follows a summer of intensified Ukrainian strikes aimed at isolating Crimea and compelling Russia to end its long-term conflict. Ukraine has particularly focused on targeting fuel tankers and energy infrastructure connected to Crimea.
With the bridge damaged, Russia has limited options and must increase traffic along key supply routes, making them vulnerable to attacks. Analysts suggest that while a sudden Russian logistical collapse is unlikely due to their evasive tactics, the growing concentration of traffic creates more opportunities for Ukrainian strikes. Ukrainian drone capabilities have been key in targeting Russian logistics, which are currently aided by favorable weather conditions.
Ukrainian forces aim to target Russian missile launchers and aircraft that threaten Ukrainian cities. The bridge linking Crimea to mainland Russia is significant, as it has been damaged previously by various attacks. A new strike on the rail section could force rail cargo through the M-14 highway, complicating logistics further. Recent attacks have already disrupted traffic on the rail side.
MD Briefing delivers expert analysis across five global fronts — the Indo-Pacific, energy, geoeconomics, European security, and the Middle East — every Monday morning. Free.
Ukraine’s forces have expanded their mid-range attack capabilities to include railway targets. With an uptick in Russian freight traffic through targeted areas, the Ukrainian military sees this as advantageous. Experts note that Russia has adapted its military logistics but faces challenges as Ukraine continues to damage infrastructure that could lead to bottlenecks.
The loss of the Crimean Bridge is seen as a blow to logistics more than to Russia’s battlefield operations. The real challenge for Ukraine is to keep the bridge disabled while applying consistent pressure to strain Russia’s supply corridor. Successfully managing both could significantly hinder Russian military effectiveness.

item.title: Before the naval drones rescued downed airmen in the Strait of Hormuz, the US Army put ...
item.summary: military and defense Before-and-after satellite images show the damage Ukraine did to Russia's Crimean Bridge. Earlier this year, the Army's DEVCOM ...
item.page_text:
Before they were rescuing downed airmen in the Middle East or detonating in Iranian ports , the US Army was looking at Saronic Corsair naval drones as a port security solution, the service said Thursday.
Earlier this year, the Army's DEVCOM Ground Vehicle Systems Center carried out evaluations of the Corsair drone at the East Coast Military Ocean Terminal in Sunny Point, North Carolina, and the West Coast Military Ocean Terminal in Concord, California, both of which are key Army shipping points for military equipment and ammunition.
GVSC explores how commercial products can be used in the Army, looking at whether they represent an emerging capability for soldiers or offer a faster and cheaper solution to a problem while meeting program requirements.
During the demonstrations, operators remotely sailed the drones around the terminals, relying on their onboard radars and cameras to get a 360-degree view of the drone's surroundings. The Corsair systems are GPS- and satellite-enabled to maintain a connection with their operators.
With each mission, the systems' autonomous capabilities learn more. "They're adding reliability each and every time they're out operating," Marco Schoener, a GVSC mechanical engineer, said in an Army release.
The drones also offered the additional benefit of reducing the burden on crewed vessels, which can come under strain. "They had issues with their boats breaking down often," Schoener said. "The idea was to supplement with something autonomous to survey and detect any surface threats on the water."
Feedback from the demos will inform the potential broader use of uncrewed systems, as well as whether Corsair systems can be employed for other Army needs.
The Corsair  a 24-foot-long surface drone developed by Texas-based Saronic Technologies  made headlines in June when it helped rescue two Army AH-64 Apache crew members off the coast of Oman after their helicopter went down during patrols . The soldiers were rescued within roughly two hours.
The vessel was operated by Task Force 59, a Navy unit focused on integrating drones and artificial intelligence into naval operations in the Middle East. US forces had practiced using sea drones for water rescue missions for years prior to the incident.
GVSC's test of the Corsair drones for port security occurred prior to the June rescue mission. According to the Army release, the Middle East operation provided a real-world example of how uncrewed technologies can support various maritime missions.
Corsair drones were also involved in attacks in July against an Iranian submarine and ship maintenance facility. Video footage from US Central Command showed three of the systems maneuvering into the port area before hitting their targets and exploding.

item.summary: "The images we use are all satellite images from Sentinel-2 , part of the European Copernicus programme. We compare images from 2023 and 2026 ...

Remember that quotation you sent out two years ago for an 18-hectare greenhouse project? The one you never heard back from? Ever wondered what happened to it? Well, the team behind Greenhouse Radar might have an answer. They developed a tool that detects new greenhouse developments through satellite imagery. "Our resolution is 10 metres, so we can see new greenhouses from about 1 hectare."
"The images we use are all satellite images from Sentinel-2, part of the European Copernicus programme. We compare images from 2023 and 2026, check each new location using AI software, and determine in which quarter a greenhouse was built," says William Simmonds of Greenhouse Radar. The data is then compared with project announcements published in various news sources.
"Where we identify an operator, it's a probable match based on size, timing and location, and we explain that on the page," William says. Every site has its own page with coordinates, before-and-after images, and a quarter-by-quarter timeline.
Started in Turkey The team started by mapping three geothermal areas in Turkey: Sandıklı, around Afyonkarahisar, and Tuzlukçu in Konya. They identified 19 new greenhouse sites on land that was still open fields in summer 2023. Together, the sites cover 101 hectares. "Only four of the 19 can be matched to a public report. The other 15 have no press coverage that we can find," William says.
Alsera's 18-hectare greenhouse near Afyonkarahisar, which opened in May 2025, appears in the imagery as a 19.6-hectare site: the ground was cleared in spring 2024, the first cover shows in late 2024, and the greenhouse was complete by spring 2025. In Tuzlukçu, two greenhouses measuring 5.3 and 3.9 hectares match reports about Agrotermal, including one HortiDaily carried in 2024 . "For a supplier, that's the difference between reading the trade press and looking at the ground. About four out of every five new sites in these areas would not have made it onto a prospect list based on announcements alone," William says.
That is exactly the audience Greenhouse Radar is targeting. Greenhouse suppliers, whether active in construction, technology, climate control, substrates, breeding, propagation or crop protection, want to know what new projects are underway and how large they are, whether they have been announced publicly or not. "And of course, financial institutions, investors and researchers," William adds. "Anyone who wants to follow a market without driving around."
The whole register is available as a free download. Morocco was added to the website last week: nine new sites covering 83 hectares have been found on imagery south of Agadir. In Ontario, three new sites totalling 36 hectares show up around Leamington and Kingsville; one is a probable match to a grower's permitted expansion, the other two have not yet been matched. The team also follows eight Canadian and two Mexican developments from public reports. A separate page lists the projects that are announced or under construction but not yet built, with the next step for each.
"Next, we're looking at the Middle East and Central Asia, and at more of North America," William adds. Interested parties can also request specific regions or work with Greenhouse Radar on a project tracker.
For more information: Greenhouse Radar [email protected] https://greenhouseradar.com

item.title: Cyclone Akvan to weaken by tonight: Rain to continue over Odisha, West Bengal
item.summary: A satellite image shows Cyclone Akvan over the east coast of the Indian subcontinent. (Photo: IMD). HEAVY RAIN, BUT NO MAJOR DAMAGE REPORTED. While ...
item.page_text:
Cyclone Akvan is rapidly losing strength after making landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha on Friday morning.
The India Meteorological Department ( IMD ) said the storm weakened into a deep depression by 11:30 am and is expected to lose more strength over the next few hours, becoming a well-marked low-pressure area by late night on November 20.
The weakening is likely to bring relief to coastal areas after the system triggered heavy rainfall and rough weather across Odisha.
Akvan crossed the north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coast close to Gopalpur between 7:30 am and 8:30 am on Friday, with sustained winds of 70-80 kmph and gusts reaching 90 kmph.
The landfall process began around 8 am and was completed by 11:20 am, according to the IMD. The storm then moved north-northeastwards across south coastal Odisha at around 24 kmph.
By 11:30 am, it had weakened into a deep depression, with wind speeds of 55-65 kmph and gusts up to 75 kmph.
The IMD expects it to weaken into a depression over the next six hours and then into a well-marked low-pressure area during the following six hours.
While Akvan brought heavy rainfall to several parts of Odisha, state officials reported no major damage or loss of life in the initial assessment.
Patrapur in Ganjam district recorded 209 mm of rainfall in 24 hours, followed by Hinjili at 207 mm, Chikiti at 199 mm and Gopalpur at 190 mm.
The downpour also affected other coastal districts, including Puri, Bhadrak and Jagatsinghpur.
The state had moved more than 3.7 lakh people to safer locations ahead of the storm, while rescue teams and emergency services were placed on standby.
Schools were also closed in several districts as a precaution.
The IMD expects Akvan to continue moving north-northeastwards across Odisha as it weakens.
The weather agency's afternoon bulletin placed the system about 40 km north of Gopalpur, 100 km west-southwest of Puri and 160 km northeast of Kalingapatnam in Andhra Pradesh.
Even as the storm loses strength, rainfall may continue in parts of Odisha and neighbouring West Bengal.
The system is expected to become a well-marked low-pressure area by late Friday night.
